newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: British army digs in again at S.African battle site.
newsitem.headline: British army digs in again at S.African battle site.

text.p: The last time the British army was in Rorke's Drift they were easier for the Zulus to spot, in their bright red jackets, shiny buttons and white pith helmets.
This time they are in dull green but still look odd in a place little changed since the British army fought what is still its most highly honoured battle here, more than a century ago.

"It's a culture shock for the Zulus to have us here and for us to be here, but we see it as an enormous privilege," said Captain Rob Dickinson, helping some 40 officer cadets build a village hall for the poor descendants of erstwhile enemies.
The only red on the first British unit to return here since the Battle of Rorke's Drift on January 22, 1879, was blisters, sunburn and brick dust swirling round the building site.
Their hall will stand just a few metres from the rebuilt Swedish Lutheran mission, where 139 of Queen Victoria's soldiers fought off a Zulu army some 4,000 strong.
King Cetshwayo's Zulus had come fresh from slaughtering 1,000 British troops earlier that day at nearby Isandhlwana.
Britain awarded a still unmatched 11 Victoria Crosses, its highest military honour, for courage at Rorke's Drift, a battle which hastened the end of an independent Zulu nation.
"Our battalion relives that day every year," said Dickinson, wearing a tee-shirt from the B Rorke's Drift Company of the Royal Regiment of Wales, whose forerunners fought there.
"We sit down every year to watch 'Zulu'," he said, referring to Michael Caine's first major film from 1963 that immortalised the battle for a generation of Britons.
The film captures the terror the tiny garrison felt as lines of Zulus came into sight, spelling near-certain doom.
Royal Engineer Colonel Andy Harris insists the choice of Rorke's Drift for his cadets' project abroad was pure coincidence. South Africa proposed it and promised there would be no hard feelings.
"I was worried we'd be seen as reliving empire links and glorifying the past. But there was no problem at all," he said.
"This is certainly not an act of atonement, it is a humanitarian project."
But the symbolism of coming back to put something into a needy community, finally free of the white rule the British army cemented here, has not gone unnoticed.
"They may all say it's just about youth programmes but to me it looks like a gesture of reconciliation," said Graeme Smythe, curator of the battlefield museum in the rebuilt mission.

"In Zulu custom after two boys fight they become friends, and if one is hurt the other cleans the wounds he has caused," Prince Gideon Zulu said as he and descendants of the battle's Zulu commander, Dabulamanzi, welcomed the British newcomers.
"We fought the British, but today we are friends."
One of the project's patrons is Brigadier David Bromhead, whose ancestor Gonville Bromhead was a commander at the battle.
Each year some 10,000 tourists, many of them British, travel the long dirt road to Rorke's Drift, some 300 km (190 miles) south of Johannesburg in KwaZulu-Natal province.

It is at the heart of a battlefield area that saw most of South Africa's conflicts, from Shaka Zulu's tribal conquests, through 19th century Boer-Zulu, Anglo-Zulu and Anglo-Boer wars to the anti-apartheid struggle and black-on-black fighting.
The tourists show more interest than locals in the battle that came as the European colonial scramble for Africa raged.
"The Zulu community here is living at subsistence level. They are not that bothered about the history and unsurprisingly they're keener to dwell on Isandhlwana," Smythe said.
Overwhelming in number and armed with captured rifles, the impis sped from their victory there to finish the redcoats off.
But the British were saved by discipline and bravery -- and also by new breech-loading rifles whose brass bullets could be reloaded far faster than the gunpowder muskets of old.
The Zulus lost 351 men, the British -- who never wore the scarlet coats of Waterloo again in a major war -- 11.
Had the Zulus, mass-mobilised to defend their country, won the battle, they still stood no real chance of winning the war.
After six months of fighting, the end came near the capital Ulundi when 2,000 Zulus were slaughtered in just half an hour.
South Africa's Zulus, now numbering nine million, had to wait more than 100 years for a real right to rule themselves again.
Elections in 1994 freed them from white rule though some complain they are now under the thumb of the Xhosa nation, to which President Nelson Mandela belongs.

But their KwaZulu-Natal region is run by the Inkatha Freedom Party of Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi -- who played his grandfather, Cetshwayo, in "Zulu", then followed his footsteps to gain real power as Mandela's most formidable opponent.
